title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
description: The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made
body: The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest."AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said. Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself."If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said."There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI."There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon."At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

schema.headline: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest

title: Esther Rantzen: The story behind Nicholas Winton on That's Life!
description: Sir Nicholas was able to rescue the mainly Jewish cohort of children after briefly visiting Prague. He was knighted in 2003 for his humanitarian work.
body: Sir Nicholas was able to rescue the mainly Jewish cohort of children after briefly visiting Prague. He was knighted in 2003 for his humanitarian work.Sir Nicholas, who was born to German-Jewish parents, made a list of the children that needed sponsorship and found homes for them to go to in Britain.He worked alongside activists and humanitarians , externalin Czechoslovakia to navigate complex political obstacles, such as getting children to Britain through the Netherlands, which had closed its borders to Jewish refugees.Sir Nicholas was ultimately successful due to a House of Commons ruling on allowing young refugees in the country, which had been passed a couple of months before his rescue mission began.With the help of his mother, he put photos of the children in British magazines such as Picture Post to help find them homes and organised for hostels to take in some refugees too.He managed to raise money to cover travel for the children and provide them with essentials when they reached British soil.His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of children he had rescued.It was given to Holocaust researchers, who helped track down some of the children he had helped.Sir Nicholas' story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988 and Dame Esther Rantzen told viewers about his story. Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement".She told The Radio Times, external he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved."I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added.She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV.They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving".Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK.She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton. The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway.Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended."That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said.The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas.That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments."In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled.This is a TV moment many will remember and in subsequent years has been rediscovered by new audiences thanks to social media.Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved".She says she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106.They would always have a connection due to the TV show, but Dame Esther said hearing the stories of the children he had saved also made her feel "immensely lucky" to have been a Jew born in England in the 1940s.Sir Nicholas' work has been the subject of a number of different films and documentaries, most recently the biopic One Life.Starring Sir Anthony Hopkins, the film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival and was released in the UK in January 2024.Dame Esther said it had been estimated "that 6, 000 people owe their very existence to Nicholas Winton".She added: "The Jewish children Nicky rescued were almost the only ones in Czechoslovakia to survive the Holocaust".And thanks to Dame Esther relaying his story to viewers on That's Life!, millions of people are now aware of the huge impact Sir Nicholas had.

schema.headline: Esther Rantzen: The story behind Nicholas Winton on That's Life!

title: Cristiano Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after boss Jorge Jesus denies rift
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time".It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earl
body: Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time".It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earlier said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-times Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.Ronaldo has said he considered retiring from international football after the World Cup in the summer but opted to continue as he chases down 1,000 career goals.He was included in Jesus' 25-man squad for the current international break and started the opening Nations League game against Wales.However, the Al-Nassr forward did not feature in Portugal's 2-1 win over Norway in Olso on Sunday and did not join his team-mates in going over to the visiting fans at the final whistle.Instead, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player headed to the changing rooms - prompting reports he was unhappy with the manager.Speaking to media before Portugal's Nations League match against Denmark on Thursday, Jesus said: "There was no incident whatsoever."Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that."Jesus said he had told Ronaldo before the match he would not be starting, but might be brought on later in the game."Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about," he added.Former Benfica manager Jesus also dismissed suggestions Ronaldo had refused to train on Tuesday, saying the 41-year-old instead had to do individual exercises for "mobility" and "strengthening" but would train as normal on Wednesday.However, Ronaldo did not join his team-mates on the pitch in Denmark with Portuguese media sharing a video of him leaving Parken stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff.And the player later took to Instagram to announce his departure."After the press conference of the national team and following a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp," he wrote."In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave."He added he wished his team-mates good luck in their forthcoming games.Goncalo Ramos scored the winner against Norway and Jesus had said the AC Milan striker would again be preferred to Ronaldo against Denmark."If I need [Ronaldo], he'll come on. If I don't need him, he won't."The Portuguese Football Federation later confirmed Ronaldo's departure in a statement which added: "Preparation for the two matches against Denmark and Norway continue as planned with the 24 remaining squad members."The entire delegation remains totally focussed on the national team's next fixtures and on achieving the established objectives."

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after boss Jorge Jesus denies rift

title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
description: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the pla
body: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped. The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes."Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane"."I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said."We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags."Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment"."Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane". The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

schema.headline: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing

title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has w
body: Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed."But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.And two of the largest AI companies in the world – Anthropic and OpenAI – are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry."There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey."And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver.""Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner". "Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins. "We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."Cyber attacks, deepfakes, and interest ratesBailey also pointed to other risks from AI, such as from the technology being used for cyber attacks.He said AI has created a "much more powerful way of uncovering vulnerabilities". "It's revealing things that have been in bits of operating software that we've had, and all of us have had." "In the wrong hands... it's a very powerful, potentially very powerful, weapon," he added.Another risk is the rise of deepfakes – AI-made pictures and videos of people that look real – which can be used to fool the public.Bailey has had first-hand experience of this. In June, deepfake images depicting him and Nigel Farage having a physical fight were promoted on social media platform X.He told the BBC that the fake images were being done in such a way that the Bank has struggled to find out where they came from."We've got to be able to trace these things back. And we need a lot of help from the tech sector to do that," he said.However, Bailey said a big potential benefit from AI is its ability of "speeding up the work that supports the Monetary Policy Committee [MPC]" which sets interest rates."It's not taking a decision, but it's a tool in the hands of the policy maker and that's good," he said.Bailey's warning came as government borrowing costs in countries including the UK, US, France and Japan hit their highest levels in decades, putting pressure on public sector finances.Governments usually borrow money by selling bonds to investors, which are a kind of IOU.The rate of return on that investment over a certain time period is called the yield. The lower the price of the bond, the higher the yield.On 30-year UK bonds, the yield rose above 6% on Thursday, its highest level since 1998. For US 10-year bonds, the yield rose to 5.34%, its highest since 2002, indicating a sell-off in the bond markets.Analyst said there was no particular trigger for this on Thursday, but central banks around the world have been raising interest rates to try to combat high inflation caused by soaring energy prices.When interest rates are high, investors tend to choose investments other than bonds, which can start to look more attractive than government debt.For example, investors have been piling into AI as firms pump money into software development and data centres, which Bailey has been warning about.

schema.headline: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns

title: Too early to say if Iran involved in Dubai-Tel Aviv flight attack, Israeli PM says
description: It is too early to say if Iran had any involvement in an attack by a pilot who stabbed another pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel
body: It is too early to say if Iran had any involvement in an attack by a pilot who stabbed another pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Israel's prime minister has said.The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, is in hospital in a stable condition, and has been hailed a "true hero" by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. One passenger, Yaniv Hayun, described how he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down.The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, where the plane took off from, Netanyahu told Fox News.Asked whether there was any indication as of now of Iran's involvement, he replied: "It's too early to say". He added that the pilot was "now being investigated in Saudi Arabia".Meanwhile, he and India's leader Narendra Modi called stabbed pilot Machchhar a "hero"."Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker - preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on X.Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code reporting a hijacking.Around 20 minutes after these codes were signalled, the plane started its manual descent for landing into Saudi Arabia. Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.Eyewitness accounts and a statement by Netanyahu confirmed one of the pilots had stabbed the other and, according to the Israeli prime minister, "apparently tried to crash" the aircraft.Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack", without giving any details. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu, and said it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.One passenger, Hayun, described how he and others on the flight had restrained the attacker."The pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door, so it was hard for us to open it," Hayun said in a video posted on social media by the prime minister's office, but before the stabbed pilot collapsed, he was able to open the door. Yaniv said he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down.He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane and after it levelled out, another pilot took over control. Airline Flydubai confirmed two on-duty crew travelling on the flight landed the plane.Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".He said: "There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event."

schema.headline: Too early to say if Iran involved in Dubai-Tel Aviv flight attack, Israeli PM says

title: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt after two injections
description: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after an attempt to execute her by two lethal injections failed, her lawyer says.He
body: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after an attempt to execute her by two lethal injections failed, her lawyer says.Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."One of her attorneys told the BBC that Pike, 50, was now "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered.Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was the subject of a last-minute legal battle.This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.Slemmer's mother May Martinez was among those who wanted the execution to take place. Speaking to NBC News after Wednesday evening's events, she said: "It was a mess."The attempted execution took place at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville at about 20:00 local time (01:00 GMT on Thursday).Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, and the curtain in the witness room was closed twice, the AP news agency reported. Media were at some point asked to leave, the news agency said.AP added that Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set. But it does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.Why there was a surge of US executions in 2025LISTEN: Could the US death penalty ever die out?In a statement reported by US media, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said he had ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred". He said the year's last remaining execution would not go ahead as planned.The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in the state in 2026 that did not unfold as planned. The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug.The Tennessee Department of Correction has said it stands by all the actions it took during the attempted execution of Pike."The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office," department spokesperson Dorinda Carter told the Tennessean newspaper. "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility," she said.Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper: "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution."We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion to stay her execution and provide medical care after the lethal injection was apparently botched.District Judge Clifton L Corker issued a ruling noting that "medical personnel have begun to administer medical care as requested in the motion".Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she likely never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure during the attempted execution."It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury," Zivot said in an email.The attempted capital punishment went ahead after multiple last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers failed.The US Supreme Court had thwarted two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection.Late on Wednesday, America's highest court overturned a reprieve granted by a lower court earlier in the day. The lower court had granted a pause, saying it needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.The Supreme Court had previously dismissed an appeal by Pike's lawyers, who had argued the jury did not get the chance to weigh mitigating evidence of Pike's documented history of childhood sexual abuse, before they sentenced her to death in 1996.The defence said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.Tennessee's governor denied a clemency request this week from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row.In her clemency petition, Pike said that she intended to beat Slemmer, not kill her, but that she was unable to "put the brakes on"."I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid," she said in a statement. "It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."The murder in 1995 created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee, after Colleen was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the symbol herself.Before the killing, Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant Shipp was 17 at the time so spared the death penalty under state law. He remains in prison.Martinez, Slemmer's mother, said at the weekend that she had waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.She told AP that a group helped raise funds for her and her husband to travel from Florida to Tennessee to witness the execution."Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said.Since 1976, when the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty, only 18 women have been executed in the US, compared to 1,663 men. That is about 1% of all US executions.

schema.headline: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt after two injections

title: Dame Esther Rantzen: Tributes paid to 'inspirational' presenter and Childline founder
description: Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006. In 2013, Dame Esther founded The Silver Line to help older people suffering from isolation and loneliness.She
body: Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006. In 2013, Dame Esther founded The Silver Line to help older people suffering from isolation and loneliness.She also led campaigns on car safety, organ donation and bullying, and later in life became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic, but last month said she was now "too physically fragile to make the journey".Burnham said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life".Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners.Baroness Jan Royall, former leader of the House of Lords and a friend of Dame Esther, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that she was a "formidable" person."She was an extraordinary, compassionate woman, a passionate woman, and she brought about such change in our world, change for the better."Baroness Royall added that Dame Esther had "a wicked sense of humour" and a "zest for life", which was the thing that "drove her to try and improve people's lives through Silver Line, Childline etc, but also with the assisted dying bill."Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told Radio 4's Today: "I was lucky enough to know her for more than 50 years, and what I remember is her energy, her intelligence, her resilience. Her vulgar streak, which she enjoyed and she said she got from her mother. She was formidable and she was fun."Dame Esther told him her campaigning was rooted in memories of difficult times in her own life as a child during and after World War Two, Brandreth said.Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning."She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said.Dame Elaine Paige, known for her roles in West End productions like Cats and Evita, paid tribute to a "great broadcaster, journalist and campaigner".She said: "Her Childline, the confidential counselling service for young people in distress, helped so many children and The Silver Line was aimed at older people suffering loneliness and isolation."Anton Du Beke, Dame Esther's partner on Strictly Come Dancing, shared a photo of the pair dancing together in the 2004 series, writing that the two had "remained firm friends" ever since.He praised her "breadth of knowledge and passion" and called her "the ultimate breaker of the glass ceiling", adding: "She will be greatly missed and my sincere thoughts are with her family."Davina McCall wrote on Instagram that Dame Esther had "made the world a better place, and inspired so many of us to do better and live life to its fullest."The message accompanied a video of the former Big Brother host discussing how Dame Esther was an "inspiration to girls like me when we were growing up".Presenter Amol Rajan said Dame Esther "changed the course of millions of lives" as he paid tribute, calling her "an inspirational, strong woman ahead of her time"."Not bad for a bright, Hertfordshire girl born during the early stages of the Second World War."Watch BBC media editor Katie Razzall's half-hour special programme Esther! on iPlayer. It will also be shown this Friday, 2 October, on BBC One at 19:30 BST.

schema.headline: Dame Esther Rantzen: Tributes paid to 'inspirational' presenter and Childline founder

title: England cricket news: Crane called up and Archer rested for Pakistan tri-series
description: Leg-spinner Mason Crane could play for England for the first time in eight years after being recalled for the one-day international tri-series in Paki
body: Leg-spinner Mason Crane could play for England for the first time in eight years after being recalled for the one-day international tri-series in Pakistan.The 29-year-old won his only Test cap against Australia in Sydney in 2018 and is now given an opportunity in the series which also involves Sri Lanka next month.Crane, who also played two T20 internationals in 2017, could also push his case in the fight to be England's number one spinner in Test cricket.Sam Curran and Adil Rashid both return after injuries, and uncapped pair James Coles and Henry Crocombe are included.Jos Buttler is out with the hamstring injury he sustained last week, while Jacob Bethell is continuing his recovery from knee surgery.Brydon Carse, who is under an investigation from the Cricket Regulator following an incident outside a nightclub in Derby in August, remains absent.———————————————————England squad for tri-series in Pakistan: Harry Brook (Yorkshire – captain), Gus Atkinson (Surrey), Sonny Baker (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), James Coles (Sussex), Jordan Cox (Essex), Mason Crane (Glamorgan), Henry Crocombe (Sussex), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Joe Root (Yorkshire), Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire).———————————————————England are on a diet of white-ball cricket until three Tests in South Africa in December as they build up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year.The tri-series in Pakistan involves the three teams taking part playing each other twice, with the top two advancing to the final. Following the trip to Pakistan, England play three one-day internationals and five T20s in Australia in November.As England continue to shape their backroom staff following the arrival of Stephen Fleming as Test coach, Jeetan Patel, Mike Yardy, David Saker and Carl Hopkinson will assist white-ball head coach Bendon McCullum in Pakistan.That means Marcus Trescothick, who took temporary charge of the Test team for the series against Pakistan in the home summer, misses the trip.It is understood the make-up of the coaching staff is part of a plan to rotate the coaches – fielding coach Sarah Taylor and fast-bowling coach Tim Southee are also not going to Pakistan.All of Trescothick, Taylor and Southee are likely to be part of England's coaching team for other tours this winter.

schema.headline: England cricket news: Crane called up and Archer rested for Pakistan tri-series

title: Captain Smit Machchhar: The 'hero' India pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight
description: Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand
body: Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022, having become an experienced pilot.Speaking to the BBC, Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, said he remembers Capt Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis. "We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."Capt Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family."Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely."In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured."His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack. "Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

title: What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel
description: At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for land
body: At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.But, speaking on Wednesday following the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane. He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar. Paying tribute to Machchhar, Netanyahu hailed him as a "true hero" and said "he saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals".Passenger Yaniv Hayun, who was later greeted and described as a hero by Netanyahu, said in a video released by the prime minister's office that he and others were trying to open the cockpit door, but the stabbed pilot was very close to it. Before the pilot collapsed, the injured man managed to open the door, Hayun said. He said that inside, the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside of the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane, explaining to Netanyahu that he watches Canadian documentary series Air Crash Investigation. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there."Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones"."There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event," he added.Yasmin Abukasis told Reuters that her daughter who was on the flight said a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor, with blood everywhere."The plane start to lose control. So all the people, they scream, they think they are going," Abukasis told AP news agency.Speaking from Ben Gurion Airport, she said her daughter phoned her to say she heard screaming as a pilot called for help, adding that two other pilots took control of the plane as other passengers ran towards a man who had a knife.Almog Itali, who was also on board the flight, told media that one of the pilots who landed the aircraft was British. The other pilot was European, Itali said, although he did not provide a specific nationality.One female passenger described the "very stressful" moment people realised the plane was descending. "We understood the pilots lost control," she told Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom."There are people here with shirts covered in blood," she said, adding: "Now we are fine and want to return home."Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.Speaking later on Wednesday, Netanyahu called the situation a "a very serious security incident".He added Israeli security forces are "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers"."I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised Machchhar's actions, calling him a hero on social media."His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy. India is proud of Captain Machchhar," Modi wrote in a statement posted on X.Flydubai meanwhile said "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".The airline said two replacement aircraft were sent to Tabuk to relieve the passengers and crew, and the incident had no impact on other scheduled operations. The repatriation flight carrying passengers left Tabuk at 17:40 local time (14:40 GMT) and arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). The spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

schema.headline: What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel

title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss
description: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.More than
body: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed. But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting. Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear."It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer."At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear."Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion."But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

schema.headline: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss

title: Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s
description: The Conservatives have said they would introduce new work requirements for under-25s claiming benefits in a "tough love" approach to youth joblessness
body: The Conservatives have said they would introduce new work requirements for under-25s claiming benefits in a "tough love" approach to youth joblessness.Under the proposals, young people who are fit to work but have not worked for six months continuously would face new rules to qualify for payments, including daily attendance at a job centre or courses.The party says the scheme would help tackle the almost one million people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are not in education, employment or training, known as Neets.But anti-poverty charity Trussell warned that people on Universal Credit can already not afford basic essentials, harming their ability to find and keep work.Under the Tory proposals, those aged 18 to 24 who apply for Universal Credit but have not previously worked for a continuous period of six months or more, for at least 16 hours per week, would instead have to take part in a "Get to Work" scheme.Rather than Universal Credit, they would receive a "Get to Work Allowance" paid at the same rate but requiring daily attendance at a job centre, on work experience or work readiness courses.They would be assigned a manager and have to take part in job search workshops and interview preparation sessions.The programme would last six months, or less if a participant secures a job - but those who are still unemployed after half a year on the scheme would have their benefit cut by 30%.Young people on Universal Credit who have previously worked for six months, have health issues or care responsibilities would be exempt.The party has also said it would look closer at whether parents' earnings and savings should be factored into welfare payments for their children.However, it said young people without parental support, including those who are estranged, would continue to have a safety net.Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the measures were designed to "show some tough love" to reduce the number of Neets."Too many young people are leaving school and signing straight onto benefits - this is a waste of their potential and a disaster for our economy," the Tory MP said.However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the Tory proposals were "deeply concerning"."We've got years of evidence of the failings of a tick-box approach. Meetings with over-stretched work coaches are already too short and often do little to actually move people into training or work," she said."We need more meaningful, good quality support, not simply more of the same."She added: "When you're struggling to pay for food and keep a roof over your head – the threat of losing financial support makes it harder, not easier, to find and keep a job."Under current Universal Credit requirements, external, people have to sign a "claimant commitment" to prepare for and look for work or increase their earnings if they are already working - but the Tories claim their rules would be stricter.The proposals were announced on Thursday ahead of the party's conference starting this weekend.Neets have been high on the agenda for political parties ahead of the imminent publication of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn on how to tackle the one-in-eight young people in the UK who not in education, employment or training.At Labour's conference earlier this week, Chancellor John Healey told party activists: "The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage."He said cutting welfare spending was a priority and announced that every mayor in England would have access to a Local Apprenticeships Service from March 2027 to generate thousands more youth opportunities.And on Thursday, the Department for Work and Pensions said every small and medium-sized business hiring a young apprentice would get £2,000 from the government under a new scheme backed by the Federation of Small Businesses.

schema.headline: Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s

title: Manchester City charges: Punishment before end of season, Premier League clubs believe
description: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told
body: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told BBC Sport.The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of its financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.They included artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" sponsorship deals.City have repeatedly denied guilt and signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by the end of this week.There have been fears that the process, which has taken three years since City were charged, could be drawn out for much longer.However, senior figures within football have told BBC Sport they see no reason why the case cannot be concluded by the end of this season.Speaking on condition of anonymity, one club official said: "It benefits everyone for this to be resolved as quickly as possible."When asked if they believed it would be, they said: "Instinctively yes, but it has to be done right."We can all see what the risks are if it's not. But those risks have been there throughout the process, as they've won the league multiple times during it."Another source said the process  "should" be resolved by the end of the season, and they hoped any appeal would be "compressed".The final decision rests in the hands of the independent commission, with the Premier League board - and City - able to suggest a suitable punishment before the panel makes its decision.There is increasingly a desire to have the case resolved by the end of the season amid fears that allowing City to get to the end of the campaign without punishment could lead to uncertainty and farce, particularly if they were to win the title.One section of the Premier League regulations says an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end, although it is unclear whether this would apply in City's case. Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.However, Ferran Soriano, the club's chief executive, has suggested the case will run for a long time.Manchester City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".Meanwhile, City club sponsor Etihad Airways said it is considering legal action against the Premier League. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".It added: "The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings."State-owned national airline Etihad, City's main sponsor since 2009, also said it was given no opportunity to engage in a process that now reflects "adversely on the airline".The statement added: "Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly. "The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision. "The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented."Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests."The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Punishment before end of season, Premier League clubs believe

title: MPs recommend BBC charter renewal is scrapped and licence fee is extended beyond TV
description: The BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV and the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent, an
body: The BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV and the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent, an influential group of MPs has said. The report from the House of Commons' cross-party culture and media committee comes ahead of the government finalising its proposals for the next BBC royal charter later this year, which will set out how the broadcaster is funded, regulated and governed from 2028.In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust. The report also said the next charter should be made permanent, so that the BBC's funding and existence is not called into question every 10 years. They said the current renewal process "creates an avoidable opportunity for political interference which has damaged the perception of the BBC's independence"."It also creates a disproportionate distraction for the BBC when it needs to be focused on its mission to inform, educate and entertain. We therefore recommend the next BBC charter be a permanent charter and not include an end date."When making recommendations about the licence fee, the DCMS said its current model was "outdated and no longer fit for purpose", and also suggested that the BBC reduced the cost from its current price of £180 per year.The committee also said the BBC should not pay "over the odds" for the rights to overseas hits such as Suits and Schitt's Creek.Although the BBC produces a lot of its own programmes, the corporation buys some international shows for its TV channels and iPlayer streaming platform.The MPs' report said the BBC could "spend more wisely when competing for programming". Overall, the BBC brings "immeasurable benefits" to society but needs reform of the TV licence fee to avoid a fate of "managed decline", they said.Committee chair Dame Caroline Dinenage said the report , externalcomes at "a pivotal moment for the BBC", which is grappling with changing media habits, declining income and negotiations with the government over how it is paid for.Dame Caroline said the government "must ensure the BBC has a universal and sustainable source of funding".But, she added, the BBC "can play its part by sweating its assets and boxing clever for the licence payer by ending illogical practices such as outbidding commercial rivals for overseas hits such as Suits, Schitt's Creek and Scooby Doo".The rights to air all three programmes were bought by the BBC after contracts with other networks or streaming services expired."At a time of constrained resources, the BBC should not be paying over the odds for overseas content, particularly when it's a bidding war against commercial UK broadcasters," the committee said.The MPs added that they "did not believe that this provides value for money for the licence fee payer".The BBC argued that it spends less than 5% of its content budget on acquiring shows, less than other broadcasters, and they are a cost-effective way of delivering high-quality content to audiences who go on to discover homegrown programming.The committee said there were "considerable challenges" for the BBC and warned that the current TV licence fee is "outdated and no longer fit for purpose".Currently, about 94% of individuals use the BBC each month but only 80% of households pay for a TV licence, the MPs noted."The licence fee should be reformed so it is no longer linked to the consumption of live TV or to a particular device, such as a television set," the committee said. "This should be an easier sell to licence fee payers if expanding the base is paired with a drop in the individual cost."The BBC's director-general Matt Brittin has previously described the current licence fee model as "a busted flush" and "yesterday's model", and has said the price could be cut if more people pay under an overhauled system.The committee also suggested the BBC should:Explore the opportunity for introducing an international TV licence so it can increase its revenue and global audienceWork with independent production companies who own the rights to many of its programmes to ensure more remain on iPlayerDevelop its current premises with facilities that can "harness the potential of new media and support the creator economy"The committee suggested the government should:Support the corporation by legislating to put a BBC button on remote controls for smart TVsPress YouTube to give a certain level of prominence for content made by the BBC and other British public service broadcastersTake back full funding for the BBC World Service, describing it as "the UK's number one soft power asset"The committee supported opening up BBC iPlayer to shows from other public service broadcasters such as Channel 4.Earlier this week, Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said, external she was open to her network's content being hosted on iPlayer.The report also called for the end of political appointments to the BBC board, to improve governance and remain trusted by the public. And the committee recommended that the BBC is given new public purposes relating to innovation and technology and combating misinformation and disinformation.The BBC welcomed the report, which it said made "some important and interesting recommendations on the future of the BBC".A BBC spokesperson said: "We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform, so we welcome the Committee's support for maintaining universal funding while overhauling the licence fee."We are also pleased to see their recognition of the vital work of the World Service, with a clear recommendation that responsibility for funding should return fully to Government."At a time of huge disruption in the media, the BBC's trust, reach and creative strength remain unparalleled. But we also recognise the need to evolve and move faster towards the future."The government's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said it "agrees entirely with the Committee's conclusion that it is in the country's best interests for the next Charter to support an ambitious and innovative BBC, and that the corporation cannot be left to a future of managed decline".A DCMS spokesperson added: "We will review and consider the committee's recommendations in detail, alongside the views of the public and other stakeholders, to inform decisions for the next Royal Charter."

schema.headline: MPs recommend BBC charter renewal is scrapped and licence fee is extended beyond TV
